claim: In Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMS), the dysregulation of both sleep-wake behavior and melatonin production strongly suggests impaired non-visual light perception.
source: In Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMS), the dysregulation of both sleep-wake behavior and melatonin production strongly suggests impaired non-visual light perception.
evidence: This claim is based on clinical observations of SMS patients and represents established knowledge about the syndrome's symptoms.

claim: Mice haploinsufficient for Rai1 were hypersensitive to light such that light eliminated alert and active-wake behaviors, while leaving time-spent-awake unaffected.
source: We discovered that mice haploinsufficient for the SMS causal gene, Retinoic acid induced-1 (Rai1), were hypersensitive to light such that light eliminated alert and active-wake behaviors, while leaving time-spent-awake unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral and EEG recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Variables pertaining to circadian rhythm entrainment were activated more strongly by light in Rai1+/- mice.
source: Moreover, variables pertaining to circadian rhythm entrainment were activated more strongly by light.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on phase shifts and circadian entrainment presented in the manuscript.

claim: The activation of rod/cone and suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) by light was paradoxically greatly reduced in Rai1+/- mice.
source: At the input level, the activation of rod/cone and suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) by light was paradoxically greatly reduced
evidence: This is supported by ERG recordings and c-FOS immunoreactivity data in the SCN presented in the manuscript.

claim: The downstream activation of the ventral-subparaventricular zone (vSPVZ) was increased in Rai1+/- mice.
source: while the downstream activation of the ventral-subparaventricular zone (vSPVZ) was increased.
evidence: This is supported by c-FOS immunoreactivity data in the vSPVZ presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vSPVZ integrates retinal and SCN input and, when activated, suppresses locomotor activity.
source: The vSPVZ integrates retinal and SCN input and, when activated, suppresses locomotor activity, consistent with the behavioral hypersensitivity to light we observed.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about vSPVZ function and inference from the experimental results.

claim: Light is the most potent environmental signal ensuring correct entrainment of endogenously generated circadian rhythms to the external 24 hr day in mammals.
source: For instance, light is the most potent environmental signal ensuring correct entrainment of endogenously generated circadian rhythms to the external 24 hr day.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about circadian biology.

claim: Light information encoded in the retina and received by the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) can reset circadian rhythm phase of overt behaviors such as sleep and locomotor activity.
source: In mammals, light information encoded in the retina and received by the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN), which harbor the master circadian pacemaker, can reset circadian rhythm phase of overt behaviors such as sleep and locomotor activity (Brainard and Hanifin, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Light directly impacts physiology, behavior, and cognition, including light suppression of melatonin, increases in body temperature, cortisol, heart rate, alertness, performance, and mood.
source: Apart from these circadian effects, light also directly impacts physiology, behavior, and cognition, including the well-known light suppression of the circadian hormone melatonin, as well as the maybe less well known light-induced increases in body temperature, cortisol, heart rate, alertness, performance, and mood (Badia et al., 1991; Cajochen et al., 1992, Cajochen et al., 2000; Leproult et al., 2001; Lewy et al., 1980; Scheer et al., 2004; Stephenson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: In nocturnal species like the mouse, light favors sleep and suppresses locomotor activity.
source: These activating effects of light are observed in diurnal species, like us, while in nocturnal species, like the mouse, light favors sleep and suppresses locomotor activity (Aschoff and von Goetz, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In SMS patients, despite unimpaired vision, a number of symptoms strongly suggest that non-visual light perception is compromised.
source: In patients diagnosed with Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMS), despite unimpaired vision, a number of symptoms strongly suggest that non-visual light perception is compromised.
evidence: This is based on clinical observations and established knowledge about SMS.

claim: SMS is a multiple congenital anomalies/mental retardation disorder associated with a heterozygous interstitial deletion on chromosome 17p11.2 in >95% of patients.
source: SMS is a multiple congenital anomalies/mental retardation disorder associated with a heterozygous interstitial deletion on chromosome 17p11.2 in >95% of patients (Edelman et al., 2007; Greenberg et al., 1991; Smith et al., 1986), or rarely with point mutations in Retinoic acid induced 1 (Rai1), a gene located within this deletion (Slager et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Common phenotypic features of SMS include obesity, self-injurious, aggressive behavior, as well as distinct craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities.
source: Common phenotypic features include obesity, self-injurious, aggressive behavior, as well as distinct craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities (Edelman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cardinal symptoms of SMS include sleep disturbances such as early sleep on- and offset, repeated and prolonged nocturnal awakening, and excessive daytime sleepiness.
source: Among the cardinal symptoms are sleep disturbances, including early sleep on- and offset, repeated and prolonged nocturnal awakening, as well as excessive daytime sleepiness (Smith et al., 1998a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The time course of melatonin levels shows an inverted rhythm in SMS patients, peaking during daytime and with low concentrations at night.
source: In conjunction with these sleep-wake disturbances, remarkably, the time course of melatonin levels shows an inverted rhythm in SMS patients, peaking during daytime and with low concentrations at night (De Leersnyder, 2006; Potocki et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Rai1 haplo-insufficiency is thought to be causal for SMS because patients with Rai1 mutations display most of the SMS features.
source: Because patients with Rai1 mutations display most of the SMS features (Edelman et al., 2007; Potocki et al., 2003), including the sleep/circadian phenotype, Rai1 haplo-insufficiency is thought to be causal (Smith et al., 1998a; Dubourg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research and represents an inference from clinical observations.

claim: Rai1 haplo-insufficient mice recapitulate some of the SMS features such as obesity and craniofacial phenotypes.
source: A mouse model for SMS has been engineered and Rai1 haplo-insufficient mice recapitulate some of the SMS features such as obesity and craniofacial phenotypes (Bi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Under LD12:12 conditions, mice of both genotypes were more active during the dark compared to the light period, reaching highest activity levels in the first 6 hr after dark onset (ZT12-18).
source: Under LD12:12 conditions, mice of both genotypes were more active during the dark compared to the light period, reaching highest activity levels in the first 6 hr after dark onset (ZT12-18; Figure 1A,B), consistent with the mouse being a nocturnal species.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The number of movements during the light phase was reduced by 67% in Rai1+/- mice compared to wild-type littermate controls.
source: The number of movements during the light phase was reduced by 67% in Rai1+/- mice, which is substantial considering that in the wild-type littermate controls locomotor activity reaches its lowest levels during this period (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The overall 24 hr activity levels were lower in Rai1+/- mice compared to wild-type under both LD and DD conditions.
source: The overall 24 hr activity levels (both under LD and DD) were lower in Rai1+/- mice compared to wild-type (Rai1+/+ vs. Rai1+/-: LD12:12: 545 ± 79 vs. 317 ± 36; p=0.019; DD: 473 ± 77 vs. 268 ± 35 movements/24 hr; p=0.006, t-tests).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: After release into DD conditions, Rai1+/- mice maintained a circadian organization of activity and rhythms free-ran with a period length slightly shorter than 24 hr, similar to wild-type mice.
source: After release into DD conditions, Rai1+/- mice maintained a circadian organization of activity and rhythms free-ran with a period length slightly shorter than 24 hr as in wild-type mice (23.8 ± 0.03 hr for both genotypes; p=0.82; t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Rai1+/- mice exhibited a more precise circadian timing of overt behaviors compared to wild-type littermates under DD conditions.
source: while analyses of the day-to-day variability of activity onset under these conditions (i.e., individual r-values for the linear regression of activity onset under DD) suggest a more precise circadian timing of overt behaviors in Rai1+/- compared to wild-type littermates (r = 0.96 ± 0.01 and 0.88 ± 0.03, respectively; p<0.05; t-test; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The phase angle of entrainment differed between the two genotypes, with Rai1+/- mice exhibiting a positive phase angle while wild-type mice showed a negative phase angle.
source: Also, the phase angle of entrainment, which quantifies the relationship between the endogenously generated circadian timing of activity and the timing of light exposure (see Materials and methods for details), differed between the two genotypes. While activity onset in wild-type mice under DD conditions occurred later than predicted by the mean activity onset under the preceding LD12:12 (−0.49 ± 0.17 hr; p<0.005; paired t-test), Rai1+/- mice exhibited a positive phase angle (+0.36 ± 0.14 hr; p<0.05; paired t-test), which significantly differed from wild-type (p<0.005; t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Rai1+/- mice showed an abrupt, 2.5 hr 'expansion' of the active phase (alpha) when released into DD, while wild-type mice showed no significant change.
source: This relative advancement of activity onset in Rai1+/- mice was accompanied by an abrupt, 2.5 hr 'expansion' of the active phase (alpha), while in Rai1+/+ mice alpha did not significantly change from that observed under LD12:12 (+18 min; Figure 1A,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,E.

claim: The magnitude of the phase advance after light pulses administered at CT22 was more than two times larger in Rai1+/- mice than in wild-type.
source: Although both light pulses resulted in the expected change in activity onset of the free-running activity rhythm, the magnitude of the phase advance after light pulses administrated at CT22, was more than two times larger in Rai1+/- mice than in wild-type (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Rai1+/- and Rai1+/+ mice showed very similar distributions of sleep and wakefulness over the 24 h day under LD12:12.
source: Time course analyses under LD12:12 revealed that Rai1+/- and Rai1+/+ mice showed very similar distributions of sleep and wakefulness over the 24 h day (Figure 2A; see also Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 6A.

claim: For none of the three sleep-wake states (waking, NREM sleep, and REM sleep) did the 24 hr values significantly differ between genotypes.
source: and for none of the three sleep-wake states (i.e., waking, NREM sleep, and REM sleep) did the 24 hr values significantly differ (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: During the light period, time-spent-awake was slightly but significantly reduced in Rai1+/- mice compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Moreover, during the light period, time-spent-awake was slightly but significantly reduced compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a striking 15-fold reduction in locomotor activity when expressed per unit of time-spent-awake during the light period in Rai1+/- mice.
source: Even so, the lower overall activity levels as well as the near complete suppression of locomotor activity by light observed in Rai1+/- mice, were not accompanied by similar changes in time-spent-awake. This dissociation resulted in a striking 15-fold reduction in locomotor activity when expressed per unit of time-spent-awake during the light period (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When Rai1+/- mice were behaviorally awake during the light period they did not leave the nest or only very briefly to drink.
source: Behavioral observation using video recordings confirmed that when Rai1+/- mice were behaviorally awake during the light period they did not leave the nest or only very briefly to drink.
evidence: This is supported by video recording observations.

claim: Quantitative analyses of the waking EEG revealed increased activity within the delta band (2–3 Hz) in Rai1+/- mice compared to Rai1+/+ mice during the light period but not during the dark period.
source: Quantitative analyses of the waking EEG revealed increased activity within the delta band (2–3 Hz) in Rai1+/- mice compared to Rai1+/+ mice during the light period but not during the dark period (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Time spent in TDW in Rai1+/- mice was reduced 2.3-fold in the light period compared to that in wild-type mice.
source: Accordingly, time spent in TDW in Rai1+/- mice was reduced 2.3-fold in the light period compared to that in wild-type mice (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When Rai1+/- mice were submitted to 60 hr of constant light (LL), mean activity levels remained continuously suppressed without marked circadian modulation.
source: When Rai1+/- mice were submitted to 60 hr of constant light (LL for 48 hr starting at the end of a 'habitual' 12 hr light period), mean activity levels remained continuously suppressed without marked circadian modulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overall activity under LL was reduced to one-fourth of the 24 hr levels under LD12:12 in Rai1+/- mice.
source: Overall activity was reduced to one-fourth of the 24 hr levels under LD12:12 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In wild-type mice, the circadian modulation of locomotor activity was preserved under LL and overall levels did not significantly differ from LD12:12.
source: This is in stark contrast to wild-type mice in which the circadian modulation of locomotor activity was preserved under LL and overall levels did not significantly differ from LD12:12 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: In neither genotype was the overall time-spent-awake changed under LL.
source: Interestingly, in neither genotype was the overall time-spent-awake changed under LL (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In Rai1+/- mice, activity levels were rapidly suppressed and reached near zero levels during each of the repeated 1-hr-light pulses under LD1:1, irrespective of time-of-day.
source: In Rai1+/- mice, activity levels were rapidly suppressed and reached near zero levels during each of the repeated 1-hr-light pulses, irrespective of time-of-day (Figure 5A,B), giving the changes in activity a distinct 'on-off' or 'switch-like' character (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In wild-type mice, while activity levels were lower during the light pulses under LD1:1, their activity levels remained well above zero and still varied according to circadian time.
source: In contrast, while wild-type mice were also less active during the light pulses, their activity levels remained well above zero and still varied according to circadian time with highest values reached in the subjective dark phase (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5A,B.

claim: Mice of both genotypes spent more time asleep during the 18 hr recovery period after 6-hr sleep deprivation, and this extra time asleep did not differ between genotypes.
source: Compared to baseline levels, mice of both genotypes spent more time asleep during the 18 hr for which recovery sleep was monitored and this extra time asleep did not differ between genotypes (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A,B.

claim: The dynamics of EEG delta power over the 72 hr recording period, including its levels immediately after the sleep deprivation, did not differ between genotypes.
source: Similarly, the dynamics of EEG delta power over the 72 hr recording period, including its levels immediately after the sleep deprivation, did not differ between genotypes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rai1 expression levels in the forebrain were remarkably stable over the day under LD12:12 conditions in wild-type mice.
source: Rai1 expression levels in the forebrain were remarkably stable over the day, in contrast to the well-known nychthemeral changes in steady state mRNA levels of the established core circadian clock genes Bmal1 and Per2, which were quantified in the same samples (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Scotopic ERG recordings revealed that retinal activation was importantly reduced in Rai1+/- mice, as evidenced by a decreased amplitude of the a-wave and the b-wave.
source: Scotopic ERG recordings revealed that retinal activation was importantly reduced, as evidenced by a decreased amplitude of the a-wave, reflecting the membrane hyperpolarization of the photoreceptors (Penn and Hagins, 1969), and the b-wave , reflecting the light response of retinal cells post-synaptic to photoreceptors (Stockton and Slaughter, 1989; Miller and Dowling, 1970) (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ERG data shown in Figures 8A,B.

claim: The general retinal morphology and histology analysis did not show any salient differences between Rai1+/+ and Rai1+/- mice.
source: The general retinal morphology and histology analysis did not show any salient differences between Rai1+/+ and Rai1+/- mice (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 9.

claim: qPCR analyses of retinal extracts did not reveal any difference in rhodopsin, melanopsin, and cone opsin mRNA levels between Rai+/- and Rai+/+ mice.
source: Consistent with the histological results, qPCR analyses of retinal extracts did not reveal any difference in rhodopsin, melanopsin, and cone opsin mRNA levels between Rai+/- and Rai+/+ mice (Figure 9O).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9O.

claim: A twofold decrease in Rai1 expression was observed in Rai1+/- mice retinal extracts.
source: We did, however, observe a twofold decrease in Rai1 expression in Rai1+/- mice, as could be expected from the haplo-insufficiency (Figure 9O).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9O.

claim: A 1-hr-light pulse administered at ZT15 induced c-FOS immunoreactivity in the SCN of both genotypes.
source: In line with previous work (e.g. [Ruby et al., 2002]), a 1-hr-light pulse administered at ZT15-induced c-FOS immunoreactivity in the SCN of both genotypes (Figure 10B,C; p<0.0001, t-tests).
evidence: This is supported by c-FOS immunoreactivity data shown in Figures 10B,C and citation to previous work.

claim: The induction of c-FOS immunoreactivity in the SCN after a light pulse was significantly reduced by ~40% in Rai1+/- mice.
source: The induction was, however, significantly reduced by ~40% in Rai1+/- mice (Figure 10B,C; p<0.005, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by c-FOS immunoreactivity data shown in Figures 10B,C.

claim: At the level of the vSPVZ, light induced a significant increase in c-FOS immunoreactivity only in Rai1+/- mice.
source: We found that compared to mice that did not receive a light pulse, light induced a significant increase in c-FOS immunoreactivity only in Rai1+/- mice (p<0.05; t-test)
evidence: This is supported by c-FOS immunoreactivity data.

claim: The number of c-FOS-positive cells in the vSPVZ after the light pulse was higher in Rai1+/- mice compared to their wild-type littermates.
source: and that the number of c-FOS-positive cells after the light pulse was higher in Rai1+/- mice compared to their wild-type littermates (p<0.05, t-test; Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by c-FOS immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Rai1 is widely expressed throughout the brain with high levels of expression observed in the olfactory bulb, cerebral cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebellum, and brainstem.
source: Rai1 is widely expressed throughout the brain with high levels of expression observed in the olfactory bulb, cerebral cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebellum, and brainstem (Toulouse et al., 2003; Bi et al., 2007; Fragoso et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: RAI1 is a highly conserved transcriptional regulator with high neuronal expression.
source: RAI1 is a highly conserved transcriptional regulator (Carmona-Mora et al., 2010) with high neuronal expression (Toulouse et al., 2003; Fragoso et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: RAI1 acts as a positive transcriptional regulator by binding to active promotor and enhancer regions.
source: and recent evidence shows that it acts as a positive transcriptional regulator by binding to active promotor and enhancer regions (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Among RAI1 target genes are Bdnf (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) and Htr2c (serotonin receptor 2c).
source: Among RAI1 target genes are Bdnf (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) and Htr2c (serotonin receptor 2c) (Huang et al., 2016; Burns et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Rai1 expression is induced by retinoic acid.
source: Moreover, as its name indicates, Rai1 expression is induced by retinoic acid (Imai et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In diurnal mammals, light information reaches the vSPVZ predominantly through the SCN relay, which inhibits the vSPVZ and is thus alerting.
source: Based on the neuroanatomical differences in the innervation of the vSPVZ by the SCN and the retina between nocturnal and diurnal rodents, Todd and colleagues Todd et al., 2012 proposed that in diurnal mammals light information reaches the vSPVZ predominantly through the SCN relay, which inhibits the vSPVZ and is thus alerting.
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous research by Todd et al., 2012.

claim: In nocturnal species, light information encoded in the retina directly stimulates the vSPVZ via the retinohypothalamic tract (RHT) and causes inactivity and sleep.
source: In nocturnal species, light information encoded in the retina directly stimulates the vSPVZ via the retinohypothalamic tract (RHT) and, overcoming the simultaneous inhibition provided by the SCN, causes inactivity and sleep (Todd et al., 2012; Schwartz et al., 2004; Watts et al., 1987; Colwell, 2011; Hermes et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: TGFα (transforming growth factor α) activates vSPVZ neurons thereby suppressing locomotor activity without affecting overall time-spent-awake.
source: Specifically, pathways regulating active waking behaviors might be good alternate candidates. TGFα (transforming growth factor α) activates vSPVZ neurons thereby suppressing locomotor activity without affecting overall time-spent-awake (Kramer et al., 2001; Tournier et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CLC (cardiotrophin-like cytokine) suppresses locomotor activity via CLC receptors on neurons localized in the periventricular region of the hypothalamus.
source: Likewise, CLC (cardiotrophin-like cytokine) suppresses locomotor activity via CLC receptors on neurons localized in the periventricular region of the hypothalamus (Kraves and Weitz, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Both TGF-α and CLC are produced in the SCN in antiphase with the daily (circadian) changes in locomotor activity.
source: Both TGF-α and CLC are produced in the SCN in antiphase with the daily (circadian) changes in locomotor activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about these signaling molecules.

claim: CLC production is stimulated by light.
source: Moreover, CLC production is stimulated by light.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about CLC.

claim: The reduced activation of the SCN observed in the SMS mouse model might have led to a reduced inhibition of vSPVZ neurons, which explains both the stronger induction of vSPVZ c-FOS immunoreactivity and the exacerbated suppression of locomotor activity by light.
source: According to this scenario, the reduced activation of the SCN observed in our SMS mouse model might have led to a reduced inhibition of vSPVZ neurons, which, in turn, explains both the stronger induction of vSPVZ c-FOS immunoreactivity we observed, as well as the exacerbated suppression of locomotor activity by light (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and the model proposed by Todd et al., 2012.

claim: In the intact mouse, RAI1-dependent signaling limits the light-induced activation of the vSPVZ thereby allowing animals to display activity during the light phase.
source: In the intact mouse, RAI1-dependend signaling thus seems to limit the light-induced activation of the vSPVZ thereby allowing animals to display activity during the light phase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: A weaker inhibition of the vSPVZ by the SCN in humans might contribute to the lower levels of alertness and attention, as well as increased day-time sleepiness observed in SMS patients during the day.
source: If also true in humans, a weaker inhibition of the vSPVZ by the SCN might contribute to the lower levels of alertness and attention, as well as increased day-time sleepiness observed in SMS during the day (Figure 11C,D) (Elsea and Girirajan, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the mouse model results and a citation to previous research on SMS symptoms.

claim: The lack of one Rai1 allele leads to a marked suppression of activity during light exposure.
source: Moreover, relative activity levels (again expressed as % of each animal's 24 hr activity under LD12:12) during rho under DD, did no longer differ between genotypes (Figure 1B,D; p=0.3, t-test), constituting further evidence that the loss of one Rai1 allele leads to a marked suppression of activity during light exposure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B,D.

claim: The suppression of activity by light depends on its intensity.
source: The suppression of activity by light depends on its intensity (Aschoff, 1960)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: At low light intensity (0.6 cds/m2), Rai1+/- mice were more active compared to the higher light level condition (6.6 cds/m2).
source: Although at these lower light levels Rai1+/- mice were more active compared to the higher light level condition, relative locomotor activity during the 12 hr light phase (as % of each animal's 24 hr activity under LD12:12 at 6.6 cdm/m2) was still greatly suppressed in Rai1+/- mice compared to their wild-type littermates (p<0.05; t-test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Activity levels of wild-type mice during the 12 hr light period did not differ between the two light intensities (0.6 and 6.6 cds/m2).
source: Interestingly, activity levels of wild-type mice during the 12 hr light period did not differ between the two light intensities.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The alpha expansion in Rai1+/- mice was already present on the first day under DD.
source: The alpha expansion was already present on the first day under DD and was due to both an advance of activity onset (consistent with the positive phase angle of entrainment) and a delay of activity offset compared to the timing of these two events on the preceding day under LD12:12 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Besides the altered light-suppression of activity, circadian entrainment by light is also affected in Rai1+/- mice.
source: These observations indicate that besides the altered light-suppression of activity (or 'masking' as it is referred to in the circadian literature), circadian entrainment by light is also affected in Rai1+/- mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on phase angle of entrainment and alpha expansion.

claim: Even at low intensity (0.6 cds/m2), light was still able to confine activity to the dark period of an LD12:12 light-dark cycle and alpha did not increase in Rai1+/- mice.
source: Even at low intensity (i.e., 0.6 cds/m2 vs. the habitual 6.6 cds/m2), light was still able to confine activity to the dark period of an LD12:12 light-dark cycle and alpha did not increase in Rai1+/- mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Rai1 haplo-insufficiency in the mouse resulted in both circadian and light-induced phenotypes while leaving the homeostatic regulation of sleep unaffected.
source: Our data revealed that Rai1 haplo-insufficiency in the mouse resulted in both circadian and light-induced phenotypes while leaving the homeostatic regulation of sleep unaffected.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Locomotor activity in the mouse can be a poor indicator of sleep-wake state.
source: The overall time-spent-awake and its diurnal distribution under standard LD12:12 conditions did not greatly differ between the two genotypes, underscoring that locomotor activity in the mouse can be a poor indicator of sleep-wake state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissociation between locomotor activity and time-spent-awake observed in the experimental data.

claim: The increase in delta activity in the waking EEG during the light suggests that Rai1+/- mice are less alert and more drowsy when awake in the light.
source: The latter observation suggests that Rai1+/- mice are less alert and more drowsy when awake in the light, and is consistent with reports of delta activity increasing progressively during prolonged waking periods in human and rat, which in human is paralleled by decrements in cognitive performance (Cajochen et al., 2002; Franken et al., 1991; Dijk et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to previous research on delta activity and alertness.

claim: The high beta/low gamma frequency band increases progressively during prolonged waking in both human and mouse.
source: This frequency range also increases progressively during prolonged waking in both human and mouse (Cajochen et al., 2002; Grønli et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The high beta/low gamma frequency band has been associated with behavioral arrest and slower movements.
source: and has been associated with behavioral arrest and slower movements (Zheng et al., 2015), as well as with the motor deficits accompanying Parkinson disease (Weinberger et al., 2009; Mallet et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The acute suppressing effects of light on time-spent-wake time were stronger in Rai1+/- mice.
source: whereas the LD1:1 experiment provided evidence that the acute suppressing effects of light on time-spent-wake time were stronger in Rai1+/- mice, as was the case for locomotor activity and TDW.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the LD1:1 experiment.

claim: The effect of light on total time-spent-awake was weaker than on locomotor activity and TDW and depended on circadian time.
source: In contrast to the almost complete suppression of locomotor activity and TDW during LD1:1, the effect on total time-spent-awake was weaker and depended on circadian time, with highest levels of wakefulness attained (or lowest suppression by light) when light pulses were given during the subjective dark phase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the LD1:1 experiment.

claim: The sleep-wake switching by light competes with the alerting signal provided by the circadian system.
source: This suggests that the sleep-wake switching by light competes with the alerting signal provided by the circadian system, as it is more difficult for light to acutely switch sleep-wake state than to rapidly alter the quality of one state (e.g. active vs. quiet wakefulness).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing circadian modulation of light effects on wakefulness.

claim: The LD1:1 protocol revealed a stronger induction of wakefulness during the 1-hr-dark pulses in Rai1+/- mice compared to wild-type.
source: In addition, the LD1:1 protocol revealed a stronger induction of wakefulness during the 1-hr-dark pulses in Rai1+/- mice compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the LD1:1 experiment.

claim: The acute, wake-promoting effect of the absence of light varied with circadian time and was largest at the start of the subjective dark phase.
source: Also this acute, wake-promoting effect of the absence of light varied with circadian time and was largest at the start of the subjective dark phase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the LD1:1 experiment.

claim: Circadian organization of locomotor activity under DD was not largely impacted by Rai1 haplo-insufficiency.
source: In the present study, circadian organization of locomotor activity under DD was not largely impacted by Rai1 haplo-insufficiency, and no differences in period length were observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on circadian period under DD.

claim: The present study's results contrast with an earlier study that reported a 13 min shortening of the free-running period in Rai1+/- mice.
source: Our results contrast with those from one earlier study in which a 13 min shortening of the free-running period was reported (Lacaria et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with a citation to previous research.

claim: Both the present study and an earlier study clearly demonstrate that circadian rhythm generation under DD is not compromised in Rai1+/- mice.
source: Despite this difference, both studies clearly demonstrate that circadian rhythm generation under DD is not compromised in Rai1+/- mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison with previous research.

claim: Rai1 haplo-insufficiency results in the transcriptional dysregulation of core clock genes such as Clock, Per2, Per3, Cry1, and Bmal1 in SMS fibroblasts and in mouse hypothalamic tissue.
source: This is surprising given that Rai1 haplo-insufficiency results in the transcriptional dysregulation of core clock genes such as Clock, Per2, Per3, Cry1, and Bmal1 in SMS fibroblasts and in mouse hypothalamic tissue (Williams et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The preferred (endogenously determined by the circadian system) earlier activity onset in Rai1+/- mice seems 'masked' by light even of low intensity.
source: Given their hypersensitivity to light, the preferred (i.e. endogenously determined by the circadian system) earlier activity onset in Rai1+/- mice seems thus 'masked' by light even of low intensity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on alpha expansion and light sensitivity.

claim: Evidence of masking of activity onset in Rai1+/- mice can be deduced from the lack of transients during re-entrainment to LD12:12 after a period of DD.
source: Evidence of masking of activity onset in Rai1+/- mice can also be deduced from the lack of transients during re-entrainment to LD12:12 after a period of DD (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Alpha compression during re-entrainment is accompanied by memory impairments.
source: Alpha compression during re-entrainment is accompanied by memory impairments (Ruby et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In Rai1+/- mice, alpha is being compressed by 2.5 hr on a daily basis under LD12:12 conditions.
source: and, assuming that in Rai1+/- mice alpha is being compressed by 2.5 hr on a daily basis under LD12:12 conditions, might also have contributed to cognitive deficits reported for Rai1-compromised mice kept under these same lighting conditions (Bi et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data and citations to previous research on cognitive deficits.

claim: The reduced response to light at the level of the retina and the SCN in Rai1+/- mice supports the idea that non-visual light perception is impaired in SMS patients.
source: The reduced response to light at the level of the retina and the SCN we report here for Rai1+/- mice, supports this idea and indicates that already at the input level, processing of light information is altered by the loss of one Rai1 allele.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and its relevance to SMS patients.

claim: The murine SMS model differs from SMS patients because mice display a striking hypersensitivity to light with respect to active waking behaviors.
source: However, at the behavioral output level, the murine SMS model clearly differs from SMS patients because mice display a striking hypersensitivity to light with respect to active waking behaviors.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and comparison with SMS patient symptoms.

claim: The contradiction between input and output effects of light in the SMS mouse model might relate to the mechanisms that determine nocturnality versus diurnality which are thought to act downstream from the SCN.
source: This contradiction might relate to the mechanisms that determine nocturnality versus diurnality which are thought to act downstream from the SCN.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data and established knowledge about circadian mechanisms.

claim: Retinoic acid signaling is a major pathway involved in eye formation.
source: Because retinoic acid signaling is a major pathway involved in eye formation (Cvekl and Wang, 2009) and other developmental processes
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: RAI1 appears to help assemble and maintain neuronal circuitry.
source: and because RAI1 appears to help assemble and maintain neuronal circuitry (Huang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The lack of one Rai1 allele is likely to impact eye development and light signaling pathways, maybe through its target gene Bdnf.
source: the lack of one Rai1 allele is likely to impact eye development and light signaling pathways, maybe through its target gene Bdnf, which is known to be important for retinal development and synaptic connectivity (Grishanin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on established knowledge about Rai1, retinoic acid, and Bdnf, supported by a citation.

claim: The SMS mouse model revealed that both circadian and direct light reception are affected.
source: The SMS mouse model revealed that both circadian and direct light reception are affected.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rai1 is a key regulator in non-visual light perception.
source: Our study thus brought new insights into the light-signaling pathways regulating behavior and suggests that Rai1 is a key regulator in non-visual light perception.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: C57BL/6Tyrc−Brd mice heterozygous for the Rai1 null mutation (Rai1+/-) were used in the experiments.
source: C57BL/6Tyrc−Brd mice heterozygous for the Rai1 null mutation (Rai1+/-) were generously provided by James R. Lupski (Baylor College of Medicine, Houston TX, USA).
evidence: This describes the experimental materials used.

claim: The Rai1 mutation concerns a 3910 bp deletion due to the insertion of a neoR-expression cassette and an Escherichia coli lacZ coding sequence into Rai1 exon 2.
source: The mutation concerns a 3910 bp deletion due to the insertion of a neoR-expression cassette and an Escherichia coli lacZ coding sequence into Rai1 exon 2 (Bi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research describing the mouse model.

claim: This mutation prevents the encoded protein from entering the nucleus thus resulting in a functionally inactive allele.
source: This mutation prevents the encoded protein from entering the nucleus thus resulting in a functionally inactive allele (Bi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the vast majority of cases, homozygosity for this mutation results in embryonic lethality.
source: In the vast majority of cases, homozygosity for this mutation results in embryonic lethality.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the Rai1 mutation.

claim: Rai1+/- mice develop obesity by week 20.
source: Rai1+/- mice develop obesity by week 20 (Burns et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the current experiments, Rai1+/- mice were not heavier than their wild-type littermates.
source: but in the current experiments, they were not heavier than their wild-type littermates (Rai1+/-: 29 ± 0.7; Rai1+/+: 31 ± 0.3 g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.
